source.title: Inferring the Size of Large Language Models From Popular Text Memorization

record.tranche_reason: The study uses neural scaling laws to motivate an exponential mapping from a memorization-based PCA index to parameter count. It does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study measures next-word accuracy on popular texts and evaluates parameter-size inference from those accuracy profiles, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy. The results below are recorded as related findings under versions ["none"]. The MoE and closed-weight lower-bound estimates do not validate the scaling-law claim and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the scaling-law idea (capability grows roughly with log parameters) to justify an exponential map from a PCA accuracy index to parameter count. It reports only how well its size-inference method performs. It never measures held-out pretraining loss against parameters, data or compute, nor compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, other modalities, or downstream predictability in the sense the versions name.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that popular-text next-word accuracy profiles give valid, conservative lower bounds on model size: valid for all 16 MoE models tested, and recovering product hierarchies for closed models. They also say the bounds are often loose, especially for MoE models, and that precise size inference remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses black-box next-word accuracy on popular texts, PCA, an exponential mapping to parameter count, and pairwise permutation tests; it does not measure the original studies' held-out-loss scaling curves or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors identify dependence on shared exposure to popular texts, domain-specific fine-tuning or catastrophic forgetting, adversarial suppression of memorization, MoE routing, safety filtering, and whether reasoning is disabled. They do not report controlled tests of these factors' effects on scaling-law exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 19 dense open-weight models (8B–405B), ln(parameters) is linear in a PCA index of popular-text next-word accuracy: R² = 0.9504, LOO R² = 0.9387, all predictions within 2× of true size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregated next-word accuracy on popular memorized texts can estimate a language model's parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: A blocked sign-permutation test on accuracy-profile differences decides which model is larger. Precision is 0.91 to above 0.83 across thresholds; recall rises from 0.87 (τ=0.01) to 0.97 (τ=0.70).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Differences in popular-text accuracy profiles support pairwise model-size comparisons.

record.problems: The study's results depend on assumptions about shared training exposure and size dominating other latent factors. It acknowledges that fine-tuning, safety behavior, reasoning, or MoE routing can distort the signal. The reported fit and validation results concern parameter-size inference from memorization profiles, not held-out loss scaling.
record.rows_left_out: The MoE and closed-weight lower-bound tables and the Appendix B text-rank correlations are not included: they concern size-estimation outputs or an exposure assumption, not the scaling-law versions in the claim.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens.
No comparison of depth, width or other shape choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling.

Next-word accuracy on memorized popular texts rises with size across mixed model families. However, it is folded into a size estimator and not reported as a downstream-task scaling curve or as a function of loss.
No test of how fitted exponents or the compute-optimal split depend on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'scaling law' is an exponential map from capability index to parameter count. It is motivated by citing Kaplan and Hoffmann, not tested against them. The rows are the study's own method-performance metrics, so the state 'observed' in the record is replaced by cannot_determine with respect to the versions. The fact that larger models memorize popular texts more accurately is at most loosely related to V6. It is not a downstream-task scaling measurement, and model families, training data and tuning all vary.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
The study's leave-one-out results predict parameter count from memorization profiles, not loss on runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens is evaluated.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count for loss.
The study concerns text models and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
No downstream-task performance is related to pretraining loss or scale.

The study discusses factors that may affect its own memorization-based size estimates, but does not test how scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on the listed fitting and setup choices.

rows.subject: 19 open-weight dense models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit an exponential mapping from the PCA index of popular-text accuracy profiles to known parameter counts.
rows.measure: Fit of inferred parameter count to PCA index
rows.note: This is a fit from a memorization-based accuracy index to parameter count, not a fit of held-out cross-entropy loss.
rows.check: This is the study's own calibration fit, from a PCA index of popular-text next-word accuracy to known parameter counts, across 19 heterogeneous instruction-tuned models. It is the study's method performance, not a loss-scaling result. No version's effect can be read from it.

rows.subject: 19 open-weight dense models (aggregate; leave-one-out cross-validation)
rows.operation_detail: Recompute the PCA axis and size curve while holding each model out, then infer its parameter count.
rows.measure: R² for inferred versus true parameter counts
rows.note: Predicts size from the memorization profile; it does not predict loss for larger training runs.
rows.check: This is the method's leave-one-out validation (R² = 0.9387) for predicting parameter count. It does not extrapolate loss to larger runs.

rows.subject: 19 open-weight dense models (aggregate; leave-one-out cross-validation)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate held-out parameter-count estimates from the memorization profile.
rows.measure: Share of predictions within a factor of two of true size
rows.note: The reported prediction target is parameter count, not held-out loss.
rows.check: This is method performance (all predictions within a factor of two of true size), not a scaling-law measure.

rows.subject: 19 open-weight dense models (aggregate; 342 ordered model pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate the blocked sign-permutation test for deciding which model is larger.

conditions.value: τ range evaluated; exact full range not stated in text

rows.value: Starts at 0.91 and remains above 0.83 across the entire range
rows.note: Reports accuracy of a relative-size inference method, not a loss-scaling result.
rows.check: This is the precision of the pairwise size test, i.e. the study's own method performance.
